claims.text: Creating a surface-enriched gradient of reactive elements enhances the high-temperature oxidation resistance of multiprincipal-element alloys.
Al, Cr, or Si can serve as the key reactive elements in the proposed surface gradient.
Surface enrichment in reactive elements promotes formation of a continuous, adherent protective oxide scale.
Processing can be engineered to enrich reactive elements near the alloy surface.
A surface-enriched reactive-element gradient produces nanoscale chemical heterogeneities.
Increasing the local surface concentration of reactive elements enhances selective oxidation.
Selective oxidation caused by surface enrichment forms a continuous and adherent oxide layer.
A continuous, adherent oxide layer reduces further oxygen ingress.
The protective oxide layer limits diffusion processes that drive rapid oxide growth or spallation.
Gradient-engineered alloys will exhibit slower oxide-scale growth than compositionally uniform alloys under identical conditions.
Gradient-engineered alloys will exhibit better oxide-scale adhesion than compositionally uniform alloys.
Gradient-engineered alloys will exhibit less oxide-scale spallation than compositionally uniform alloys.
A homogeneous reactive-element distribution is expected to produce a less optimal and more discontinuous oxide scale.
The proposed behavior should hold for multiprincipal-element alloys containing Al, Cr, or Si at 1000–1200 °C.
Diffusion is the dominant mechanism in the stated 1000–1200 °C regime.
The quantitative relationship among gradient steepness, diffusion kinetics, and oxide-scale quality requires experimental calibration.
